words: Giri's Red Hat
Giri had a hat. It sat on a mat.
A cat ran at the hat. Snap!
The cat sat on the hat. Giri ran.
Giri had a plan. Giri had ham.
The cat ran at the ham. Giri had the hat back.
Giri and the Cat
A tan cat sat on Giri's mat.
Giri had ham in his bag.
Giri sat. Then the cat sat.
The cat ran at the ham. Snap!
Giri sat back. Then the cat sat on his lap. A nap at last!
Giri and the Jam
Giri had a pan of jam.
"That jam is for the ham," he said.
An ant ran at the jam. It sat in the jam!
Giri had a fan. He can fan the ant.
The ant ran. So Giri had the jam and the ham.
Giri's Nap
It was a day for a nap.
Giri sat on a mat. The cat sat too.
"I can nap," said Giri.
Tap, tap! An ant ran at his hand.
Giri and the cat ran. Then a nap at last!
Giri and the Hen
A white hen sat on ten eggs.
One egg had a wiggle. Then a big wiggle!
Crack! Now a wet chick! It is pink.
The chick did not sit. It ran in a big net.
Giri held it. All is well. One white chick!
Giri's Big Dig
Giri had a big dig. Dig, dig, dig!
Clink! What is in the pit? A tin lid!
The lid had a map. What can this be?
"I will dig again!" Dig, dig, dig went Giri.
A red gem! "Do it again!" Giri came back.
Giri and the Bed
Giri had a rip in his red bed.
"I know I can fix it!" He had a pin.
When did he fix it? Fast, fast!
A cat sat above the bed. An ant ran in.
There! The rip is hid. The bed is best!
Giri's Tin Lid
The tin lid fell. Clink! It hit the rim.
Giri hit the lid. "This is a bell!" Ding, ding!
A red hen ran in. She can tap!
Her taps and his taps were a hit.
Ding! Tap! "We are a band!" said Giri.
Giri and the Pot
Giri had a pot on a log.
Plop! A frog hid in it. Its name was Fizz.
Ten frogs hid in it! "What is this about?"
Many frogs sat on the rim of the pot.
"It is their pot!" Giri had a story to tell.
Giri and the Pup
A pup dug in the mud. "How much mud!"
"Does the pup want a bath?"
Giri got a tub of suds. Some got on the pup!
Rub, rub! The mud runs off. Fun!
The pup is not in the mud. Giri is also wet!
Giri and the Dog
Drip, drip. Mud dots on the path.
Giri went dot to dot. Dot, dot, dot.
At the end sat a lost dog on a log. Pant, pant!
Giri got broth and a snug rug. The dog slept.
Not lost. The dog is with a pal.
Giri's Hot Cup
Giri set a hot cup on the rug. Bad plan!
The cup fell. The rug got wet, wet, wet.
Mop, mop, mop! The spot is not wet.
Then the cat sat smack on that spot. Cats!
Next cup: not on the rug.
Giri and the Bun
Giri met a bun on a rug. The bun had legs!
Run, bun, run! It ran past the cat and the hen.
Snap! Giri got the bun at last.
The legs? Ants! Six ants had the bun.
Giri splits the bun with the ants.
Giri Gets Wet
Splish, splash! Giri got in a big tub of suds in the sun.
Suds on his legs. Suds on his chin. Fun!
Then Giri sat on a hot mat. Drip, drip.
The sun did its job. Giri got dry.
Wet, then dry. The sun wins.
Giri and the Box
The big tan box went buzz, buzz, buzz!
Is it a bell? Is it a jet? Giri did a check.
A red bug! It sat on his hand. It did not bite.
Zip! The bug flit off.
A box can hold a big shock!
Giri's Big Run
Giri ran. The pup ran. A big run in the hot sun!
Pant, pant! Run, run, run!
The pond! Giri got in. Splash! The pup got in. Splash!
In the end, the pond won.
The best end to a run is a splash.
Giri Bakes a Cake
Giri had a grand plan. He wanted to bake two cakes for his pal Jay.
But the cake stayed flat in the pan. It did not lift a bit!
"Wake up, cake!" Giri gave the pan a brave shake. He saw it stay flat. "Oh no!"
He did not wait. He got the flat cake out and made a stack: cake, jam, cake, jam!
Jay ate it by the lake. "Make me two, Giri!" That flat cake was the best.
Giri and the Speedy Boat
Giri had a small boat. He hoped to row home while the stream was slow.
But the boat did not float! It sat low by a big stone. "What is in here?"
Giri gave it a shove. No go! What did he find? Two toads! They had made it a home!
"Take this home, toads!" Giri made them a moss home on the stone.
The toads hopped off. The boat rose and rode the foam home!
Giri Helps the Bee
Giri met a weak bee by a green tree. It was too weak to see its way home.
The bee could not reach its nest. "I need a good rest," it said with a weep.
Giri had a plan. "A leaf can help! A leaf can lift you up!"
He set the bee on a green leaf. "This should reach the tree," said Giri.
The bee sped up to see its nest. A good deed, and a good day!
Giri's Big Day
Giri climbed a high hill with his bright kite. He would fly it across the wide sky.
But the sky was still. No wind! The kite fell to the side. "Come on, wind!" he sighed.
Giri held the line tight. "I will run to make the wind!" And he did.
His run made the wind rise! The kite went up high, across the bright sky.
By the water, Giri sat with a smile. "Come and see my kite fly!"
Giri and the Snail
Giri met a small snail on the trail one wet day in May.
The snail sat in the way of a drain. Cold rain fell fast on the trail.
"Wait, snail!" Giri put out his hand and gave it a soft push, off the trail.
The snail slid to a safe spot, out of the cold rain. Giri waited all the way.
The snail waved its tail. "I love this snail," said Giri. "It may take all day!"
Giri Makes a Kite
Once upon a time, Giri had a fine plan to make a kite. He had made kites before.
He tied the strings tight, but the kite fell on its side. It had no tail!
Giri sighed. "This kite will not fly because it has no tail," he said.
He cut one white stripe, then the other, and tied both tight to the kite.
Now the kite had a fine tail! It rose high, white as salt in the sky.
Giri's Bike Ride
Giri went on a bike ride along a wide white lane in the sun.
The bike hit a rock! Giri slid off and bumped his side. "Who left this here?"
A young pup came by. "Are you sad?" Giri wiped his face.
He rode on until he felt fine. Then he went back to give the lane a fix.
Giri rolled the wide rock off the side. "Now the lane is safe to ride!"
Mrs Tan Flies a Kite
Mrs Tan had a white kite. "I made it when I was nine," she said.
"Can you still fly it?" said Jay.
Up, up, high in the sky!
Jay held his line tight. His kite dipped. Giri ran fast. His kite fell on its side.
Mrs Tan did not run. She let the line out bit by bit, and waited for the wind.
Up, up, high in the sky!
The white kite rose up and up, highest of all. "I am not nine," said Mrs Tan, "but the wind is the same!"
Who Took the Lime Pie?
Jay made a lime pie for his mum. He set it on the side and went to ride his bike.
When he came back, a big slice was missing! "Why?" he cried. "Who did this?"
Lime pie, lime pie, who took my lime pie?
Not Giri. He was asleep. Not the cat. She did not like lime.
Then Jay spied Mum, with a bright smile and a bit of pie on the chin.
"I had to try it," said Mum. Jay grinned. "That is fine. It was for you!"
Giri and the Goat
One day, Giri met a goat on a road. It had left its mother and brother.
The goat had a bite of Giri's soft coat! "That is not something to eat!"
"Hold on, friend! Do not become a wolf!" Giri held out a big pile of oats.
The goat gave up the coat and chose to chomp on the tasty oats.
Giri went home with his coat. The goat ran to its mother and brother.
Giri at the Beach
Giri went to the beach to see the green sea. A girl and a boy came too.
A wave reached his feet! He leaped back with a squeak. "That was just too quick!"
"We must run from the wave!" The girl and the boy ran with Giri up the beach.
Then the wave went back. "It is tag with the sea!" They all leaped in and back.
They had a sweet peach treat. What a day at the sea!
Giri and the Rain
Giri was on a long gray trail one calm day in May. He said it would stay hot all day.
A big rain came fast! "Where can I hide?" Giri got wet on the trail.
"Wait it out!" He hid in a cave to watch the rain. Drip, drip, drip.
The rain stopped. Giri made big mud prints all the way home. Stamp, stamp!
Giri saw his trail of prints. "Where the rain fell, I had fun!"
Giri's Green Seed
Giri had a green seed. "Maybe it will be a tall tree," he said.
But the seed did not seem to wake. Giri gave it a nod of his head and waited.
His friend came by. "A seed may need a deep drink each day." So Giri gave it a drink.
He let it feel the heat of the sun. At last, a green leaf reached up!
The seed has a friend in Giri. Maybe it will be a tree!
Giri's Cosy Home
Giri went to make a cosy home in a stone cave by an old oak tree.
A nosy mole dug a deep hole in the stone wall. It ate its way right in!
Giri went to fill it. "A hole can be of use! Do not throw it away."
He made the hole a note slot and let a note go down to the mole.
Now Giri and the mole have a way to chat. Notes go to and fro!
Giri and the Flute
Giri had a flute. He liked to play a tune in the cool shade.
One day the flute made no tune. It had been full of grit and dust.
Giri used a cube of soap and a tub of suds. "This will make it new," he said.
Soon the flute played the same sweet tune as before. The notes came out true.
By the green tree, people sat to see him play. "Play the same tune!" they would say.
Giri's New Kite
Giri drew a plan for a new kite with a deep blue pen.
The wind blew and blew. His old kite flew into a tree and got stuck. "Please help!"
Giri made the new kite. He glued the frame and tied each stick tight.
"Is your kite pretty?" asked his pal. "It is! And each bit is blue," said Giri, happy.
The new kite flew up, up! "Please fly!" Giri felt so happy. "The best kite yet!"
Giri and the Moon Pool
One night Giri went to the pool to see the moon shine like a plate.
A grey mist hid the moon. "Do not leave!" Giri said to the moon. The pool went dim.
Giri sat to keep still. Two flies zoomed by. He ate a snack.
Soon the mist swept away. The moon came back and lit up the sea.
This night, this moon, this pool — Giri will keep these in mind. Time to leave!
Mei Ling's Loose Tooth
Mei Ling had a loose tooth. It was at the front, and it went wiggle, wiggle, wiggle.
She tried to pull it. No. She tried to push it with a spoon. No. She chewed and chewed.
Wiggle, wiggle, will it go? Not yet, no!
At lunch, she had a huge bowl of noodles. Giri pulled a funny face, and she had to giggle.
Plop! Into the noodles went the tooth. "It is true," said Mei Ling. "A new smile, just in time!"
Shoo, Goose, Shoo!
Jay went to feed the ducks at the pool. Soon a huge goose came up to him.
Jay went home. The goose went too. Jay ran down the road. The goose flew after him!
Shoo, goose, shoo! What do you want me to do?
Jay ran to his room and shut the door. Tap, tap, tap! The goose was at the window.
Then Jay spotted the crumbs. They fell from the hood of his blue coat. "So that is the food you want!" he said, and gave it a snack.
Giri and the Shell Shop
Giri went to the shell shop. Shells sat in a big box on a shelf.
Bash! The box fell off the shelf. Shells slid across the shop.
"I can fix this myself!" It did not take much time. He got a brush and a bin.
He put the shells back in the box. Flick! A moth in it began to fly.
The man was so glad. This shop was his life! He held up a shell to the light.
Giri Sings a Long Song
Giri had a song to sing in class. He sang it with a quick clap and a click.
At the test run, Giri got stuck. The song went wrong. Nothing at all!
He did not quit. "Why did I stop?" He shut an eye and sang from the top, big and strong.
He sang high and long. The song was fine! Clap, click, sing along!
Then the song was a hit! His pals sang along, strong and long.
No. No. Also No.
Mole did not want to go out. "No. It is cold. I will stay home."
"Come and play," said Giri. "We can jog to the lake." "No. Also no. Still no."
"Does Mole want a hot bun? I have two buns from home." A pink nose came out.
"So... one bun is for me?" "Yes!" Out came Mole. No coat. No hat.
"See? It is fun out here." "The bun is why I came. But yes — also the fun."
No. No. Also No. (A Play)
Narrator: Mole was at home, under a big stone. / Giri: Come and play, Mole! / Mole: No. It is cold. I will stay home.
Giri: We can float a boat on the lake! / Mole: No. Also no. Still no. / Narrator: Giri held up two hot buns.
Giri: Does Mole want one? / Narrator: A pink nose came out. / Mole: So... one bun is for me?
Giri: Yes! / Narrator: Out came Mole. No coat. No hat. / Giri: See? It is fun out here.
Mole: The bun is why I came. But yes — also the fun.
The Bee and Me
"I see a bee!" said Giri. "And the bee sees me!"
The bee went from tree to tree. "Wait for me! I want to see what you can see."
"Then keep up! We need to find the sweet spot." Giri did not see it. "Here? Is it here?"
The bee sat still on a green stem. "Take a deep sniff." Sweet! A bed of mint!
"Great find! You and me — we make a fine team." "Yes," said the bee. "Buzz!"
The Snail Race
Jay had a snail named Blue. Giri had a snail named Pine. Today was race day by the lake.
Slow and low, go, snail, go!
Pine shot off fast. Blue was slow, slow, slow. Jay gave a sigh.
"Keep going, Blue!" said Jay. Then Pine stopped to eat a green leaf. And another. And another!
Slow and low, go, snail, go!
Blue crept on, inch by inch, past the leaf and past the line.
The winner was Blue! "Soon Pine will need a nap," said Giri, "on a full tummy!"
Giri and the Big Storm

Giri was at the farm when dark skies came over the barn. The storm burst with a crash. The barn door banged hard in the wind. His own star chart, which he wrote out by hand, blew off the wall and landed in a puddle by the yard.

Giri ran to the barn. The door was stuck. He pushed and pulled with all his might. At last, the door swung open. Giri grabbed the star chart and ran back in. The storm passed and the sun lit the yard once more.
Giri hung the chart to dry. He was not going to buy a new one. He felt glad he had not given up.
Giri Finds a Star

Not long ago, Giri walked far from the farm one night. The sky was very dark and clear. A large bright star fell from above and landed near the river, though he was the only one to see it. Giri hurried over to find it.
The star was stuck under a fern by the water. Giri bent down and picked it up. It was warm and gave off a soft glow. A bird chirped from a branch as if to say well done.
Giri held the star close and walked home with a warm glow in his heart.
Giri and the Clever Bird
A thrush sat on a branch and watched Giri from above. Giri had lost his shell necklace on the path. He searched in the thick bushes and checked behind each rock, but did not find any of it.

The thrush gave a sharp chirp. It hopped to a patch of grass and pecked at something shiny. Giri rushed over. There was his shell necklace, half hidden under a thin leaf. Giri picked it up. "I don't know how you knew!" he thanked the clever bird.
Giri clipped the shell necklace on. Both he and the thrush felt glad. The thrush goes where it likes, and Giri set off home into the sunshine.
Giri at the Market

Giri walked to the market to get a jar of honey for his mother. The stalls were bright with herbs, berries, and fresh corn. A trader called out, "Best herbs here!" The market began to get busy, but Giri could not see the honey stall.

He turned a corner and there it was, tucked between a herb cart and a butter stall. Giri picked out a large jar and paid the farmer with his change. On the way home he spotted a perfect red pepper, good to eat, and got that as well.
Giri gave the jar and the pepper to his mother. Her frown became a big smile. "You begin to shop like a pro!" she said.
Giri and the Blue Bin

Giri walked home from school and stopped by the blue bin. The bin was full of tins and sheets of paper. Giri had a juice box in his bag. He knew it should be saved, but was not really sure whether it should go in the blue bin.

He checked the chart on the bin. "Juice boxes — yes!" it said. Giri tried to crush the box flat to make it fit. The box sprang back and bumped his chin. After a few more tries, with both hands, the box went flat with a crunch.
Giri pushed the flat box in through the slot. The bin made a clang, like a note of music! Giri walked home and felt glad he had done the right thing.
Giri Helps a Neighbour
Giri heard a knock at the door. It was Mrs Tan from the flat next door. Her light bulb had burnt out and her step stool was broken. She could not reach the top of the shelf, which was very high.

Giri offered to help. First he stood on his tiptoes, but he was not quite tall. Then he hurried to his flat and brought back a firm step stool. He set it in place inside her door, climbed up, turned the old bulb out, and put a new one in. He did not move until the light burst on!
Mrs Tan clapped and gave Giri a warm kueh to say thank you. Giri felt glad he had helped a neighbour in need.
Giri at the Farm

Giri spent the morning at the farm with his grandfather. The chickens scratched in the yard and the sheep sheltered under a large shed. Giri always helped to fetch fresh water from the well and fill the bucket for the horse. It was hard work, but he liked it.

After lunch, a chicken got out at a gap in the fence. Giri set off after it, past the barn and behind the shed. At last, he got it by the cherry tree, just as his aunty waved from the shed. He carefully shut the gap with a thick branch.
Grandfather smiled. "Sharp thinking, Giri," he said. Giri felt glad to be a real farm helper.
Giri's First Errand

Giri's mother asked him to go to the corner shop to get butter and yoghurt. It was his first errand on his own, and he wanted to help his family today. Nerves ran through his body as he walked, turning left at the big curb and then right at the fir tree.

At the shop, Giri picked up the butter, but he could not find the yoghurt. A helper in a purple shirt led him to the third shelf, behind a stack of tins. Giri held his bag open and put everything in. On the way home, a bird chirped above him as if to cheer him on.
Giri handed the bag to his mother. "Perfect!" she said. Giri grinned from ear to ear. His first errand was a success.
Giri and the Baby Turtle

Giri was at the beach one morning when he spotted a baby turtle stuck in a dip in the sand. The turtle had turned the wrong way. It was far from the water, and the hot sun had made the sand burn below its flippers.

Giri worked fast. First, he dug the sand away from the shell. He did not try to carry it; instead he turned the little turtle to face the water. The turtle began to stir. It pushed with its flippers, slid along the wet sand, and swam off into the surf.
Giri stood and stared until the turtle was finally just a dot in the sea. His first rescue! He walked home with a warm glow inside.
Giri's Garden Surprise

Giri had a little garden plot by the void deck. He planted a row of seeds between two stones and stirred the dirt with a small fork. It was not easy, but he often gave the seeds a drink of water and waited.

Weeks went past, but nothing came up. Giri felt glum. Then, after a big rain, he spotted something green. A funny little turnip top! Soon ten green tops stood in a perfect line. Giri turned the dirt and let them grow bigger and bigger.
At last, Giri pulled up ten firm turnips. He gave three to Mrs Tan, and when his work was done, his mum cooked the rest for dinner. His first harvest was the best surprise.
Giri's Helping Day
On Sunday, Giri helped all day long. In the morning he started with the dishes, washing and stacking them in a shining row. Then he dusted the shelf and folded the clean clothes.

After lunch, Giri kept helping. He watered all eight plants and picked up the blocks. Mrs Tan needed a hand with her shopping bags, so Giri carried the lightest one up the steps. He could feel his feet getting tired, but he kept smiling.
At dinner, Mum smiled and said, "You helped all day. You must be the kindest helper in the city!" Helping, Giri decided, was a great kind of fun.
Could You? Would You? Should You?
A small bird sat on the fence and did not stir. "Could we fly to the barn?" said Giri. "I could," said the bird, "but should I? A storm is coming. I can smell the rain."
"Would she come if I marched along?" said Giri. "She could ride on my arm." The bird looked at the dark sky. "We should not go far," she said. "Let us get under cover first."
Big drops of water started to fall. Giri and the bird darted under the cart by the farm. The storm passed over them with a roar. Then the sun came back and lit up the yard.
"The bird had it right," said Giri. "Could, would, should — think hard first!" "Yes," said the bird. "That is why I am a smart bird."
The Missing Badge
It was the morning of the school march. Mei Ling had a purple badge for her shirt, but now it was missing. "I had it in the first lesson!" she cried.
Giri helped her hunt for it. They checked under the bench, behind the hedge and in the kitchen. They looked in the porch and by the sports shed. Giri even turned out his own bag. No badge!
Then Mr Lim stepped up with his phone to take a photo of the class. "Smile, Mei Ling!" he said. Mei Ling turned to face him, and Giri burst out giggling.
"Look — the badge!" said Giri. It was pinned to the back of her hat the whole time. Mei Ling went pink, then marched off with a big grin.
Giri at the Fair

The annual fair had arrived and the whole town was buzzing with joy. Giri joined the crowd and walked past stalls selling toys, popcorn, and bright balloons. A pair of clowns juggled on the main stage while children pointed and cheered.

Giri spotted a chair-mending stall at the far end. An old carpenter was repairing a wooden chair with care. One leg had a nasty crack. Giri watched as the carpenter oiled the joint and tapped a fresh dowel into place.

"Would you like to try?" the carpenter asked. Giri took the mallet and gave the dowel one careful tap. It slotted in perfectly. The carpenter nodded and smiled. "You have a fair hand for this work," he said.
Giri walked home through the evening air, feeling proud. He had discovered a new skill and made a new friend — all in one joyful afternoon.
Giri and the Joyful Noise

Giri was walking through town when he heard a loud, joyful sound coming from the community hall. He followed the noise and found a crowd of people singing and clapping. A woman in a brown coat was leading the group.

"Come and join!" she called out. Giri felt a bit shy. He sat on a stool by the window and listened. The voices bounced around the room — high, low, loud, and soft. The sound made him feel warm inside.

At last, Giri stood up and joined in. His voice was small at first, but it grew louder with each note. Soon it rang out loud and proud, bouncing round the hall. The woman gave him a proud nod. The whole group swayed and sang until the sun went down.
Giri walked home humming the tune. He had found something that brought him joy — the power of voices joined together.
Giri Repairs the Chair

An old rocking chair sat in the stairwell of Giri's block. It had been there for as long as anyone could remember. The seat was bare, the armrest had a tear, and the paint was wearing thin. No one seemed to care about it any more.

Giri decided to repair the chair. He searched his grandfather's workshop and found sandpaper, glue, and a spare plank. First he glued the cracked armrest. Then he sanded the seat until it was smooth. Finally he cut the plank to replace the broken slat at the back.
It took two afternoons of careful work. When the chair was done, Giri placed a small cushion on the seat and set it by the corridor window where the air was fresh.
Mrs Tan from next door sat down and sighed with happiness. "This is the best seat in the block," she declared. Giri beamed. A little care had turned something forgotten into something shared.
Giri Hears a Cheer

It was the last day of the school year. Giri sat near the window, feeling a small knot of fear in his chest. His friends were moving to different classes next year. Would he still see them? Would they forget about him?

The bell rang and Giri walked out to the field. The grass was clear and green in the sunshine. Then, from behind the canteen, he heard a cheer. "Giri! Over here!" He ran towards the sound and saw all his friends gathered under the old rain tree.
They had set up a small farewell party — sandwiches, lemon cordial, and a hand-drawn card with each friend's name. "We will always be near, even if we are not in the same room," said Mei Ling.
Giri felt a tear of happiness on his cheek. He looked around at the smiling faces. This was not an ending — it was the beginning of something dear that would last for years to come.
Giri's Sports Day

It was Sports Day. The whole school poured out onto the field. Flags snapped in the wind, and the crowd on the bleachers made a joyful roar. Giri was in the relay team. He bounced on his toes at the starting point, trying to shake off the doubt in his stomach.

The whistle blew. The first two runners sprinted down the track. When the baton reached Giri, he gripped it and ran with all his power. Halfway round the bend, his foot hit a mound of soil. He stumbled, fell, and felt the grit sting his knee.

For a moment the noise around him seemed to fade away. Then the crowd found their voice. "Go, Giri! Get up!" Giri pushed himself to his feet and ran on. He was not the fastest, but he crossed the line with the baton held high.

His team did not win a trophy, but they won something better — the loudest cheer of the day. Giri felt proud. Courage, he decided, was not about never falling down. It was about getting up and carrying on.
Giri and the Treasure Map

Giri found an old piece of parchment stuffed inside a drawer at his grandmother's house. It was a hand-drawn map with a dotted line, a compass, and one word: "Treasure." Giri's jaw dropped. Could this be real?

He followed the map across the lawn, past a pair of palm trees, and down a narrow stairway to the canal path. The trail led to an old wall covered in crawling vines. Near the base, a small wooden box was half-buried in the earth.

Giri knelt and carefully pried the lid open. Inside he found a faded photograph of his grandmother as a girl, a pair of pearl earrings, and a short letter. "To the one who finds this," it read, "you have the same spirit of adventure that I had. Take care of it."
Giri sat back on his heels, awed. The treasure was not gold or jewels — it was a story, a memory, and a connection to someone he loved. He carried the box home with the greatest care.
Giri Goes to Town
On Saturday, Giri took the bus to town with his mum. The town was loud and busy. Crowds moved up and down the street, and the smell of fresh bread drifted out of a baker's shop.
Mum gave Giri two dollars to spend. He counted the coins in his palm and looked round the stalls. So many choices! A round bun? A cold drink? A small brown mouse toy with a long tail?

Then Giri spotted an old man selling paper windmills that spun round and round in the wind. One windmill was painted gold and brown, with a loud little clack as it turned. Giri handed over his coins without a doubt.
On the bus home, Giri held his windmill up high and let it spin. Round and round it flew! A windmill that turns all day, he decided, was money well spent.
Giri Draws at Dawn
Giri woke up before dawn one morning. The sky was still dark, and the air was cool. He took his pencils and paper down to the lawn, sat on the damp grass, and waited for the sun.

Slowly, the sky began to change. Streaks of pink and gold crawled over the rooftops. A hawk soared past on wide, still wings. Giri drew it all — the dawn light, the yawning town, the small black cat creeping along the wall.
His hand moved fast. He drew the lawn, the lamp posts, and the last pale star before it faded. When he looked down at his paper, the whole morning was caught there in pencil lines.
At breakfast, Giri showed the drawing to his mum. "You saw all that at dawn?" she said, in awe. Giri nodded. The best part of the day, he decided, was the part most people never saw.
Giri and Scout

Mrs Tan from next door was going away for the weekend. "Could you take care of Scout for two days?" she asked Giri. Scout was her small brown dog with one floppy ear and a tail that never stopped wagging.

Taking care of a dog turned out to be real work. Scout needed fresh food and clean water, a walk in the morning, and a walk at night. He barked at the lift and chased his tail on the stairs. Giri had to keep him away from Mrs Tan's plants!
But on the second day, something changed. Scout curled up beside Giri while he read his book, one ear up, fast asleep. Giri scratched the soft fur behind it and smiled.
When Mrs Tan came home, Scout ran to meet her. "He looks so happy and well cared for!" she said. Giri felt proud. Caring for a pet was hard work — and worth every minute of it.
Giri and the Coin Jar
Giri kept a coin jar on his desk. Every day he dropped in the coins left in his pocket, and the jar grew heavier month by month. He was saving up for a big red robot from the toy shop in town.
Every Sunday, he counted his coins out loud. "A dollar. Two dollars. Three dollars and twenty cents!" He was proud of every coin in that jar.

Then one day, walking home past the school, Giri spotted his mum outside the flower shop. She was looking at a pot of orchids. She smiled at the flowers, then looked at the price and walked on. That night, Giri stopped counting his coins for the robot. He had found something better to buy.
On Sunday, Giri proudly handed his mum the pot of orchids. Her mouth fell open, then curved into the widest smile. "My boy!" she said. Some things, Giri decided, count more than any toy.
Who Is on the Stairs?
Mrs Tan was away for the night, so Scout was staying with Giri. At bedtime, Scout would not settle. He sat by the door with his ears up and let out a low growl.

Then Giri heard it too: a scratch, a thump, and a soft little noise from the stairs. His heart pounded. Was it a thief? He grabbed his torch, took a deep breath, and crept out to the stairwell with Scout.

There, on the stair below, sat an old cardboard box. Giri shone his torch inside, and his jaw dropped. A mother cat lay curled up in the box, and beside her were four tiny kittens, no bigger than a sock.

Scout did not bark. He lay down near the box and gave a soft whine, as if to say, "Careful. They are scared." Giri paused, then gave a quiet cheer. His brave, loyal dog had not been growling at a thief at all. He had been guarding them.
Giri brought out a bowl of water and an old towel for the box. In the morning, Mrs Tan came home and found a happy surprise: her dog had a new job. Scout was a kitten guard, and he was proud of it.
How Giri Found Out

A loud sound rolled up from town to the hill where Giri stood. He looked around. A big brown cloud was rolling down the hill — and it was coming his way! "What is that? How big is it? What do I do NOW?"

"I must find out about that cloud," said Giri. He did not run. He did not hide. He marched down the road to find out for himself. The sound got louder and louder. The cloud got rounder and rounder. Giri counted his steps out loud to stay brave. "One. Two. Three. Four."
Then Giri found out. It was not a cloud at all! It was a crowd — a crowd of kids from town, kicking up dust as they bounced a big round ball down the hill. "Come and join us!" they shouted.
Giri let out a proud shout: "I found out by myself! A thing is not so big when you find out about it." He joined the crowd, and the game was loud, round, and fun.
Giri Rides the MRT
Giri got on the big red MRT. The MRT was fast.
The MRT was full. Giri had no seat.
Giri held on to the rod and did not slip.
A kind man let Giri sit in his seat. Giri sat and felt glad.
Giri got off at his stop and gave a big grin.
Giri's First Day at School
It was Giri's first day at school. He had a big red bag.
Giri lost his peg. He did not know where to put his bag.
Giri ran to look in each room.
A kind pal led Giri to his peg. Giri hung his bag up.
Giri sat at his desk and felt glad.
Giri at the Hawker Centre
Giri came to the hawker centre to get his mum a treat.
He got lost in the maze of lanes and stalls.
Giri went from lane to lane and looked at each stall.
A nice auntie smiled and led him to the noodle stall. Giri gave a wave and paid.
Giri went home with the noodles. His mum gave him a huge smile.
Giri and the New Year
It was the New Year. The lane was full of red lights and gold flags.
Giri lost his mum in the big crowd.
Giri called out, "Mum! Mum!" He ran up the lane.
Giri spied the red light of the stall. His mum waved to him.
They sat and ate sweet kueh. Giri felt glad.
Giri at Deepavali
It was Deepavali. The street had bright oil lamps and gold clay pots.
Giri's oil lamp went out in the wind.
Giri cupped his hands to keep the flame safe.
A kind auntie came and lit the lamp. The lane shone bright once more.
Giri sat and ate a sweet treat. He felt glad.
Giri at Gardens by the Bay
Giri went to the Gardens by the Bay to see the tall Supertrees.
A small bird got stuck in the garden net.
Giri called for a park ranger to help.
Giri got a long stick and helped the bird get free. The bird flew up with a chirp.
Giri looked up at the stars and felt a warm glow in his heart.
The Lost Key
Giri was at the park when he saw a shiny key on the path. The key had no name on it. He looked around the park to see if anyone was searching, but the path was empty and no one was near.
Giri picked up the key and put it in his shirt pocket. He walked to the ranger hut and showed it to the park ranger. "I will help find the owner," said the ranger. He pinned a note on the park board.
Giri felt glad he had not left the key on the ground. Someone out there needed it to get home.
The ranger put up a paper on the park board: "Found: one key. Ask at the hut." Many people came to ask, but none had the right key. Giri and the ranger checked each person one by one.
A boy tried to grab the key and run. Giri called out, "Stop! That is not yours!" The boy gave back the key. Giri felt firm and fair. It was important to make sure the key went to the right person.
Giri and the ranger went on looking. They were sure the right owner would come.
The next day, an old man came to the hut with a sad face. He said he could not find the key to his flat. Without it, he could not get home. Giri showed him the key they had found.
The old man could not remember what his key looked like. His eyes were not clear. They tried the key in his lock. It fit! The old man gave a shout of joy. "You are a good boy!" he said.
Giri walked home and felt a warm glow of pride. A kind act is never too small.
The Night Market

One evening, Giri's street began to change. Vans pulled up, and stalls grew along the road like mushrooms after rain. By sunset, strings of little lights hung between the lamp posts. The night market had come to town.
Giri walked through the market with wide eyes. Stalls sold cold drinks, warm kueh, and sizzling snacks. Smoke curled up from a satay grill, and somewhere a bell rang again and again.
Then, near the last stall, Giri heard a sound that made him stop and turn. Somewhere close by, someone small was crying.
Behind the last stall stood a small girl with tears on her cheeks. She had lost her father in the crowd. "I turned round and he was gone," she sobbed. "I cannot find him."

Giri remembered being lost once, and how scary it had felt. "Hold my hand," he said. "We will find him together." They walked to the satay man, who lifted the girl up high and called out in a booming voice, "Whose girl is this?"
A man burst out of the crowd with wide, worried eyes. He hugged the girl tight and shook hands with Giri again and again. As they rode away on the bus, the girl waved at Giri through the window.
Giri walked home under the strings of lights. The market was loud and bright, but the best part of the night was the small hand that had held his.
Giri's Week in Penang: Day 1

Today Mum, Grandpa and I flew from Singapore to Penang. It was my first time on a plane, and I held the arm of my seat all the way up. Then I looked out of the window and forgot to be scared. The clouds looked like a field of white cotton.

When we landed, the air was hot and sticky, just like home. We took a taxi over a long bridge that went across the sea. Grandpa pointed at the water. "When I was a boy, there was no bridge," he said. "We took a slow ferry, and I was sick the whole way."

Penang is where Grandpa grew up. In the afternoon, we walked down the street where his family had a shop. The old shophouses were painted pink, green and yellow. Grandpa stopped in front of a blue door and was quiet for a long time. "This was our shop," he said at last. "My father sold rice and sugar here." Now it sells cold drinks and ice cream, so we had some.

For dinner, we went to a busy hawker centre by the sea. Grandpa ordered a plate of char kway teow for me. The noodles were dark and smoky, with prawns and bean sprouts on top. The cook tossed them in a huge pan over a roaring fire. It was the best thing I have ever eaten, even though it made my tongue tingle.

Now I am in bed, and Grandpa is snoring in the next room. Before he went to sleep, he winked and said, "Tomorrow, we go hunting." I asked him what we were going to hunt, but he just smiled. I will find out in the morning.

Now I know what Grandpa meant. We went hunting for paintings! In George Town, artists have painted pictures on the walls of old buildings, and you can walk around and find them. Grandpa gave me a paper map with little red dots on it. Each dot was a painting.

We started early, before it got too hot. The first painting was a boy on a swing, reaching up to the sky. The second was a cat so big that it covered the whole side of a house. I had to stand far back to see all of it. My favourite was two children riding a real bicycle that was fixed to the wall. I sat on the bicycle seat, and Mum took a photo of me.

By lunchtime, my legs were tired, so Grandpa waved down a trishaw. A trishaw is a bicycle with a seat for two people at the front. The rider pedalled us slowly through the narrow lanes while I held the map. Every time I spotted a painting, I shouted, and he rang his bell.

In the afternoon, we cooled down with a bowl of cendol. It has green jelly noodles, red beans, coconut milk and lots of shaved ice. Grandpa says it tastes the same as when he was small. I believe him, because he finished his bowl before I had eaten half of mine.

Back at the hotel, I counted the red dots I had crossed out. Eleven! Grandpa only found nine, but he says he walked down these lanes every day as a boy, so his dots count twice. I said that is not how counting works. He just laughed.

Today we went up Penang Hill. There is a special train that climbs straight up the side of the hill. It is so steep that the seats are built like steps. When the train started to move, I pressed my nose to the glass and watched the town get smaller and smaller below us.

At the top, the air was cool and fresh, and it smelled of trees and rain. We walked along a path in the forest. The trees were so tall that I could not see the tops of them. Mum showed me a tiny lizard on a branch. It was the same green as the leaves, and it did not move once.

Then we came to a lookout point. From there, I could see the whole island: the bridge we drove over on Monday, the old town with its red roofs, and the sea all around, shining in the sun. Grandpa put his hand on my shoulder. "When I was your age, I came up here with my father," he said. "Now I am here with you." I did not know what to say, so I just held his hand.

We were sitting on a bench to eat our snacks when a monkey jumped down from a tree. Before anyone could move, it grabbed the bag of peanuts out of Grandpa's lap and ran back up the trunk. It sat on a branch above us, eating our peanuts one by one, and looked very pleased with itself.
Grandpa says the monkey must be a relative of mine, because it also eats too fast. Tomorrow we go to the beach. I am going to keep my snacks in my pocket.
How the Kingfisher Got Its Blue Coat

Long ago, when the world was new, the kingfisher was a plain little bird. His feathers were the colour of mud, and nobody looked at him twice. The other birds had bright coats. The parrot was red and green, the sunbird was yellow, and the peacock had a tail full of eyes. The kingfisher sat on his branch by the river and wished that he could shine like them.

One morning, the Sky leaned down to look at herself in the river. As she bent over, a blue bead fell from her necklace and dropped into the water. It sank down, down, down, to the bottom of the deep, dark river. The Sky cried out. "My bead! Who will bring back my bead?"

The parrot said, "I cannot swim." The sunbird said, "The water is too cold." The peacock said, "My tail would get wet." Only the little brown kingfisher said nothing. He stood on his branch, took a deep breath, and dived straight into the river like an arrow.

It was dark and cold under the water, and he could not see. But he kept going, kicking with his feet, until his beak touched something smooth and round. He grabbed the bead and shot back up into the sunlight, dripping and shivering, and placed it in the Sky's hand.
The Sky was so pleased that she gave him a coat of bright blue, the colour of her own morning. The setting sun saw what he had done, and painted his chest a warm orange to match.

That is why the kingfisher is blue and orange today. And that is why, even now, he still sits by the river and dives into the water again and again. He is checking that nobody else has dropped a bead.
